title: Tenant latency regression detection and circuit-breaker runbook
author: Priya Menon
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook describes the detection, automated mitigation, and operator playbook for tenant-facing latency regressions in private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It codifies SLO thresholds, Prometheus alert rules, automated circuit-breaker actions, customer-impact scope checks, communication templates, and post-incident validation. The goal is to reduce user-visible latency degradations and provide predictable, reversible mitigations that preserve correctness and compliance.

Scope and audience
------------------
- Scope: Redwood private deployments (VPC-connected control plane and on-prem runtime). Covers model serving request latency for tenant routes (generation/chat/embeddings) and the orchestration of fallback/circuit-breaker actions.
- Audience: Field operators, SRE on-call, Private Deployments support engineers, Customer Success for escalations.

Why this matters
-----------------
- Latency regressions are the most visible SLA breach to product teams; they can be caused by cache eviction, kernel changes, autoscaling anomalies, noisy neighbors, or model swap regressions.
- Automated detection + conservative circuit breaking prevents noisy tenants from degrading cluster-wide SLAs and provides a safe tripping mechanism while preserving customer data isolation guarantees.

Key definitions and SLOs
------------------------
- Tenant P99 request latency (100–4096 token requests): target <= 150ms (soft), alerting threshold >= 250ms sustained over 5m (actionable), critical >= 500ms sustained over 3m (escalation).
- Request error rate (5xx) should remain < 0.5% per tenant per 10m window.
- Circuit-breaker: an automated traffic-steering policy that routes affected tenant traffic to a compatible fallback model variant (quantized, smaller model) or to a degraded QoS path (strict token-rate limit + shorter max length) to preserve availability.

Detection signals and alert rules (examples)
-------------------------------------------
- Primary PromQL alert examples (adapt and localize to customer metric names):
  - Latency surge (actionable):
    ALERT TenantLatencySurge
    IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime\",tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[5m])) by (le)) > 0.25
    FOR 5m
    LABELS {severity=\"page\"}
    ANNOTATIONS {summary=\"Tenant {{ $labels.tenant }} p99 latency >250ms for 5m\"}

  - Critical latency regression:
    ALERT TenantLatencyCritical
    IF histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{job=\"runtime\",tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[3m])) by (le)) > 0.5
    FOR 3m
    LABELS {severity=\"page\"}

  - KV cache miss storm:
    ALERT KVCacheMissStorm
    IF sum(rate(kv_cache_miss_total{tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[2m])) by (tenant) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{tenant=~\"$tenant\"}[2m])) by (tenant) > 0.2
    FOR 2m

- Secondary signals: pod restarts, GPU throttle metrics, enqueue Q length, model swap events, storage I/O saturation. Use these to reduce mean time to root cause.

Escalation and ownership
-------------------------
- First responder: current SRE on-call for private deployments.
- If ticket requires customer communication, assign Customer Success engineer and the private-deploy field lead.
- Security or data concerns: immediately notify Security on-call (see incident communication templates).

Automated mitigation (circuit-breaker) design
--------------------------------------------
The circuit-breaker is implemented as an orchestrated policy with three selectable mitigations. It must be enabled by default with conservative triggers and always log signed evidence for compliance.
- Mitigation A (transparent): reduce tenant concurrency (token/inference rate) by 30% and enable strict prefix KV cache favoring hot keys. Fastest, reversible.
- Mitigation B (fallback model): route traffic to a verified smaller/quantized model variant with compatible API. Preserves functionality at lower throughput cost. Use when cache-based mitigations fail for 3m.
- Mitigation C (degraded QoS): enable per-request truncation to 512 tokens and enforce 1s hard timeout before returning partial results. Use for customer-accepted emergencies only.

Automated action sequencing (recommended)
1. On TenantLatencySurge alert (5m): trigger Mitigation A automatically. Create incident ticket with auto-populated diagnostics.
2. If latency remains above actionable threshold after 3m post-MitigA: execute Mitigation B and notify CS with pre-filled customer impact template.
3. If Mitigation B fails to restore latency within 3m or errors increase >0.5%: notify lead SRE and on-call; consider Mitigation C after manual approval.

Sample circuit-breaker API calls (pseudo-CLI)
---------------------------------------------
- Apply concurrency throttle:
  curl -X POST https://controlplane.internal/api/v1/tenants/$TENANT/circuit-breaker \n    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' \n    -d '{\"action\":\"throttle\",\"concurrency_pct\":70,\"reason\":\"auto-latency-surge\"}'

- Swap to fallback model variant (safe swap):
  redwoodctl swap-model --tenant $TENANT --from model-id:1.2.0 --to model-id:1.1.0-quant --grace-period 30s --kv-preserve true

Operational triage checklist (operator steps)
-------------------------------------------
1. Validate alert -> confirm tenant p99 abnormality in telemetry and check correlated signals (KV miss, pod CPU, GPU mem, restarts).
2. Review recent control-plane events (model swap, canary rollout, config change) in the last 60 minutes.
3. If Mitigation A not yet applied, allow automation to run; if already applied, escalate to Mitigation B.
4. Run quick k8s health checks on serving pods:
   - kubectl -n runtime get pods -l tenant=$TENANT
   - kubectl -n runtime logs <pod> | tail -n 200
5. If fallback model active, validate output quality against a small prompt-set (run local eval harness):
   - echo 'Quality check prompt' | redwoodctl eval --tenant $TENANT --model fallback-model-id
6. If restored, follow post-incident remediation steps (below). If not restored, open high-priority incident channel and assign action owners.

Customer communication templates (short forms)
--------------------------------------------
- Initial acknowledgement (within 15m):
  Subject: [Redwood] We are investigating increased latency for your deployment
  Body: We are seeing elevated request latency for your tenant (p99). Our automated mitigations may be active temporarily. This may result in slower responses or shorter outputs. We will post updates every 30 minutes until resolved.

- Status update (after mitigation applied):
  We have applied a temporary traffic shaping and, if needed, a fallback model to preserve availability. We will share detailed diagnostics and next steps in the follow-up report.

Post-incident remediation and follow-up
--------------------------------------
- Root cause analysis (3–7 days): collect traces, KPIs, model artifacts, and control-plane logs. Document RCA in the internal incident tracker with corrective actions and owners.
- Remediation examples: kernel rollback to previous runtime build, KV cache size increase, model quantization tuning, tenant-specific QoS policy adjustments.
- Regression guard: add the triggering prompt set to the model-onboarding/regression suite and schedule a canary for future model swaps.

Testing and game-day validation
------------------------------
- Quarterly drills: simulate a 2x KV miss storm across a synthetic tenant to validate automated mitigation sequencing and customer comms.
- Add automated unit tests for circuit-breaker policy enforcement and audit trail generation in the CI pipeline.

Telemetry and evidence retention
-------------------------------
- Retain 1Hz request traces + 1s histograms for the tenant for 14 days for post-mortem. Store signed mitigation decision logs for compliance (30 days default, configurable per customer contract).

Ownership and runbook maintenance
--------------------------------
- Runbook owner: Private Deployments SRE (on-call rotation).
- Review cadence: Every 6 months or after any major change to runtime, model catalog, or control plane.

Appendix A — Quick PromQL snippets
----------------------------------
- Tenant p99 over 5m: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{tenant=\"$T\"}[5m])) by (le))
- KV miss ratio: sum(rate(kv_cache_miss_total{tenant=\"$T\"}[2m])) / sum(rate(kv_cache_requests_total{tenant=\"$T\"}[2m]))
